notes.summary:
Dispersion tells how spread out the values are around the centre. Two data sets can have the same mean and very different spread. Paper 2 asks 8 to 12 questions here: range, quartile deviation, mean deviation, standard deviation and variance, the coefficient of variation, combined SD of two groups and the effect of adding or multiplying by a constant.

Absolute measures (range, QD, MD, SD) are in the units of the data. Relative measures (coefficients, CV) have no units and are used to compare two series.

concepts.title: Absolute and relative measures
concepts.body:
Absolute measureRelative measure (unit-free)
Range = L − SCoefficient of range = (L − S) ÷ (L + S)
Quartile deviation = (Q3 − Q1) ÷ 2Coefficient of QD = (Q3 − Q1) ÷ (Q3 + Q1)
Mean deviation about ACoefficient of MD = MD ÷ A (A = mean or median)
Standard deviation σCoefficient of SD = σ ÷ x̄; coefficient of variation = (σ ÷ x̄) × 100

Use absolute measures to describe one series and relative measures to compare series with different units or very different means.

concepts.title: Range and quartile deviation
concepts.body:
• Range = largest − smallest. Quick, but depends only on two extreme values. Used in quality control and for daily share prices and temperatures.
  • Interquartile range = Q3 − Q1; it covers the middle 50% of the data.
  • Quartile deviation (semi-interquartile range) = (Q3 − Q1) ÷ 2. Not affected by extreme values and can be found for open-end classes.

Mini example: 12, 7, 25, 18, 3. Range = 25 − 3 = 22. Coefficient of range = 22 ÷ 28 = 0.79.

concepts.title: Mean deviation
concepts.body:
Mean deviation (average deviation) = Σ|x − A| ÷ n, where A is usually the mean or the median. For a frequency table, MD = Σf|x − A| ÷ Σf.

  • Signs are ignored (absolute values), which is its main weakness for algebra.
  • Mean deviation is least when taken about the median.
  • Mini example: 4, 7, 9, 10, 15. Median = 9, absolute deviations 5, 2, 0, 1, 6, total 14. MD about median = 14 ÷ 5 = 2.8.

concepts.title: Standard deviation and variance
concepts.body:
SD is the root of the mean of squared deviations from the mean. It uses every value and suits further algebra, so it is the best and most used measure.

  • σ = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ n) = √(Σx² ÷ n − x̄²). Variance = σ².
  • Frequency table: σ² = Σfx² ÷ N − (Σfx ÷ N)².
  • Step deviation: σ = h × √(Σfu² ÷ N − (Σfu ÷ N)²), u = (x − A) ÷ h.
  • SD of the first n natural numbers = √((n² − 1) ÷ 12). For 1 to 7: √(48 ÷ 12) = 2.
  • SD of two values a and b = |a − b| ÷ 2.
  • Root mean square deviation s = √(Σ(x − A)² ÷ n) and s² = σ² + (x̄ − A)². So the RMS deviation is least (equal to σ) when A = x̄.

Mini example: 4, 8, 10, 12, 16. Mean 10, squared deviations 36, 4, 0, 4, 36, total 80. Variance = 16, SD = 4.

concepts.title: Effect of origin and scale
concepts.body:
If every value is changed to y = a + bx:

MeasureAdding a constant aMultiplying by b
MeanIncreases by aMultiplied by b
Range, QD, MD, SDNo changeMultiplied by |b|
VarianceNo changeMultiplied by b²
CVChangesNo change (if b > 0)

So σy = |b| σx and Var(y) = b² Var(x). Example: σx = 4, y = 7 − 3x gives σy = 12 and Var(y) = 144.

concepts.title: Coefficient of variation
concepts.body:
CV = (σ ÷ x̄) × 100. It is a percentage, so it compares spread across series with different means or units.

  • Lower CV = more consistent, more uniform, more stable.
  • Higher CV = more variable, less consistent.
  • Mini example: Batsman A mean 50, SD 10 gives CV 20%. Batsman B mean 40, SD 6 gives CV 15%. B is more consistent even though A scores more.

concepts.title: Combined mean and SD of two groups
concepts.body:
Groups of sizes n1, n2 with means x̄1, x̄2 and SDs σ1, σ2:

  • Combined mean x̄ = (n1x̄1 + n2x̄2) ÷ (n1 + n2).
  • d1 = x̄1 − x̄, d2 = x̄2 − x̄.
  • Combined variance = [n1(σ1² + d1²) + n2(σ2² + d2²)] ÷ (n1 + n2).

The d² terms matter: two groups with the same SD but different means give a larger combined SD.

concepts.title: Comparing the measures
concepts.body:
• For any data: SD ≥ MD about mean ≥ MD about median, and SD is never negative.
  • For a normal (symmetric bell) distribution: QD ≈ (2/3)σ and MD ≈ (4/5)σ, so 4 SD = 5 MD = 6 QD roughly.
  • In a normal distribution, mean ± 1σ covers about 68.27%, ± 2σ about 95.45%, ± 3σ about 99.73% of the values.
  • SD = 0 only when all values are equal.
  • Lorenz curve is a graphic measure of dispersion for income and wealth.

varieties.name: Range and quartile deviation
varieties.how: Range = L − S. QD = (Q₃ − Q₁) ÷ 2. Coefficients divide the difference by the sum.

example.q: Q₁ = 20 and Q₃ = 50. Find the quartile deviation and its coefficient.

varieties.name: Mean deviation
varieties.how: Find the mean or median, take absolute deviations, add them and divide by n.

example.q: Find the mean deviation about the median of 4, 7, 9, 10, 15.

varieties.name: Standard deviation and variance
varieties.how: Find the mean, square each deviation, average the squares (variance), then take the square root. Or use Σx²/n − x̄².

varieties.name: Coefficient of variation
varieties.how: CV = σ ÷ x̄ × 100. The lower CV is more consistent.

example.q: Batsman A: mean 50, SD 10. Batsman B: mean 40, SD 6. Who is more consistent?

varieties.name: Combined mean and SD
varieties.how: Find the combined mean first, then the gaps d₁, d₂ of each group mean from it, then use [n₁(σ₁² + d₁²) + n₂(σ₂² + d₂²)] ÷ (n₁ + n₂).

example.q: Group 1: 60 values, mean 40, SD 5. Group 2: 40 values, mean 50, SD 5. Find the combined SD.

varieties.name: Change of origin and scale
varieties.how: Ignore the added constant. Multiply SD, MD, QD and range by |b| and variance by b².

example.q: The SD of x is 20. Find the SD of y = (x − 100) ÷ 5.
steps: Subtracting 100 does not change the SD.

tips: Variance = mean of squares − square of mean: σ² = Σx²/n − x̄².
SD of the first n natural numbers = √((n² − 1)/12); variance of 1 to n = (n² − 1)/12.
Mean deviation is least about the median; the sum of squared deviations is least about the mean.
Lower CV wins every "more consistent" or "more uniform" question.
For two groups, compute the combined mean first; forgetting the d² terms is the commonest mistake.
For a normal distribution, QD : MD : SD ≈ 10 : 12 : 15 (from QD = 2σ/3 and MD = 4σ/5).
traps: A negative multiplier still gives a positive SD: use |b|. Variance uses b², which is always positive.
Do not add a constant to the SD when every value is shifted; only the mean moves.
Variance is in squared units; SD is in the original units.
QD is half the interquartile range, not the full Q₃ − Q₁.
A larger SD does not mean less consistent when means differ; compare CVs instead.

formulas.name: Mean deviation
formulas.expr: Σf|x − A| ÷ N,  A = mean or median

formulas.name: Combined variance
formulas.expr: [n₁(σ₁² + d₁²) + n₂(σ₂² + d₂²)] ÷ (n₁ + n₂),  dᵢ = x̄ᵢ − x̄

formulas.name: Linear change
formulas.expr: y = a + bx ⇒ σy = |b| σx, Var(y) = b² Var(x)

questions.q: If 10 is added to every observation of a data set, its standard deviation:
questions.solution: Adding a constant shifts every value and the mean equally, so the deviations x − x̄ stay the same. SD is unaffected by change of origin.
